title: 5-Minute Quickstart
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 5-Minute Quickstart Goal: hear why Impulse Anvil exists before learning all of its controls. The whole idea: your sound goes into the plugin, an impulse response (IR) changes it, and Impulse Anvil lets you redesign that response. Using the free demo? Follow Steps 1–5. They teach the core A/B → Time Morph → Edit workflow with demo-available features. Steps 6–7 use the full relationship/authoring system and WAV baking. 1. Put Anvil on a track Use a sound you already know well: drums, voice, guitar, piano or a synth. A fairly dry source makes the transformation easiest to hear. Keep the listening level sensible while experimenting. Unusual IR material can create strong resonances. 2. Load something into A Click Load in A, or drag a compatible audio file onto the A panel. If you do not have your own IRs, use a factory IR. A compatible recording can also be useful creative material even when it is not a controlled acoustic measurement. Click the A panel and listen to what the loaded response does to your track. Notice: you are not editing the original vocal, drum or synth. You are editing the response that transforms it. 3. Add B and hear Time Morph Load something obviously different into B. Contrast makes the next step easier to hear. Click the Morph panel , choose Time Morph , and move Morph . A and B are material. Morph decides the relationship between them. Notice: at different Morph positions, the prepared response changes. Your track is now being transformed by that changing response. 4. Change one source before Morph Return to A or B. Move Time slightly, listen, then try one small Color change. The demo gives you one Color row per IR, which is enough to hear the distinction. Notice: this changes A or B itself before Morph decides how the two prepared sources relate. 5. Keep only the useful part Open EDIT and move Start and End around the part you want. Start before End = forward Start after End = reverse link them = scan one fixed-size window through the IR Shift + drag = fine movement Ctrl + drag = very fine movement Make the response shorter until the character you like is still there but unnecessary tail is gone. FREE DEMO PATH COMPLETE Continue with the full workstation You now understand the core signal flow. The next two steps use full-license features: the complete Morph relationship library, A→B Lerp/Draw and WAV baking. 6. Choose — then draw — a deeper relationship Keep A and B unchanged and switch from Time Morph to one other relationship. Try Spectral for a different kind of blend or Common to emphasize what the responses appear to share. Then return to Time Morph , enable A→B Lerp , choose Draw , and paint one obvious movement between A and B. Notice: first you changed what relationship Anvil creates. Then Draw made the relationship depth change inside the response itself . When Draw makes sense, continue to Path, Glue and Omni → 7. Bake it When you hear something worth keeping, press Bake . The full version writes the result as a WAV IR. You can load it back into Anvil, combine it with something else, or use it in another compatible convolution plugin. You have learned the core loop Material → relationship → movement → sculpt → Bake. You do not need to understand every Morph mode before experimenting. Want school-like tasks instead? Open Guided Learning →

title: Acoustic Bodies & IR Comparison
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Creative workflow Acoustic Bodies & IR Comparison Yes: an instrument body can become useful convolution material. No: one IR is not a complete clone of the physical instrument. This page answers the practical version of the question: what can you learn or create if you capture the response of a guitar body, violin body, cabinet or other resonant object? Can a guitar-body IR make an electric guitar sound acoustic? A body response can impose some of its captured resonances and filtering onto a DI electric-guitar signal. That can move the tone toward a body-like acoustic character and can be very useful creatively. It will not fully turn the electric guitar into the measured acoustic guitar. A real acoustic instrument also depends on string/bridge/body coupling, radiation in different directions, microphone position, playing dynamics and behaviors that one fixed linear impulse response does not contain. Can I tap or click the body and record it? For creative sound design, a clean tap/click recording can absolutely be interesting material. For a controlled comparison, use the most repeatable excitation and recording setup you can: same position, same microphone, same gain, same room and as little background sound as practical. A casual tap recording should not be presented as a laboratory measurement. It can still be a great IR-design source. Can I compare two guitars or violins? Yes - especially when both captures were made under matched conditions. Load one into A and the other into B, then choose the question: Common - what response component appears shared? Unique A / Unique B - what remains characteristic of one side after estimated shared material is removed? Aligned Difference - what is left after main events are aligned and subtracted? Matched Residual - what remains after alignment and broadband level matching? Difference Focus - where do they disagree most? Spectro-Temporal Residual - where do differences change across both time and frequency? Transfer - what stabilized filter-like operator describes movement from A toward B, or B toward A? Can this tell me why an old expensive violin sounds better? It can help you hear and inspect differences in the captured linear response . It cannot prove why one instrument is better, more valuable or preferred. Construction, radiation, dynamic behavior, performer interaction and the measurement setup itself all matter beyond one captured IR. Treat the result as one acoustic view of the instruments, not a verdict. Can I add only the part of B that A does not already have? Unique B is the closest direct answer. It estimates what remains characteristic of B after the component shared with A is removed. This is useful when B has a crisp, resonant or spatial quality you want to study without simply crossfading the entire B response over A. It is not semantic magic: capture timing, level and environment influence what the algorithm sees as shared or unique. If the two recordings were made very differently, some of the "difference" may be the measurement rather than the instrument. Bake the useful relationship Once the relationship sounds useful, Bake it. That lets you audition the extracted or transformed response as its own WAV IR, compare it later, or load it back into Anvil for another generation. Practical rule: use matched captures for comparison; use anything interesting for creative sound design.

title: Bake & Export
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Bake & Export Bake means: Keep this IR. Whatever prepared response you are hearing can be turned into a reusable WAV. What Bake keeps Bake can include: A or B preparation Time Color and Texture per-slot Normalize and Gain Morph A→B Lerp authored routes: Draw, Path, Glue or Omni Start/End slicing or reverse slicing fades and Pre IR In EQ Width final IR Normalize IR-side Limiter What Bake does not keep These controls only affect how the plugin plays on your track: Input Wet Level Dry / Wet Out Export format Impulse Anvil writes the result as a 32-bit floating-point WAV . After export The completion window shows where the file was saved. Press Show File to reveal it directly in Explorer. Use the result anywhere A baked IR can be: loaded back into A or B combined with another Anvil Bake used in another compatible convolution plugin used in an IR loader that accepts standard WAV impulse responses This is where recursive design starts: A + B → Bake C C + D → Bake E E + recording → Bake F Baking Lerp and authored routes There is one visible Bake button. If A→B Lerp or an authored route is part of the prepared result, Bake includes it. Draw writes relationship movement into the ordinary output timeline. Path renders forward/backward source-time travel using its horizontal-distance clock. Glue Path appends separate painted pieces and owns its duration independently of Lerp Start/Time. Omni Path uses the selected Lerp source window while horizontal and vertical 2-D route travel both create output time. Bake commits the resulting prepared construction exactly as used by the prepared Preview path. Technical background Bake writes the current prepared IR as 32-bit float WAV. The prepared-IR chain is bounded by a 30-second safety budget at ordinary sample rates. Final track playback mixing happens afterwards and is not embedded in the WAV.

title: Bend Time with Path
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Bend Time with Path Path can move through the Lerp source-time in both directions. One IR can move forward, return to earlier material, then continue forward again. Goal Create an IR with replayed or reversed internal time sections while the A/B blend changes at the same time. Build it Load A and B. Enable A→B Lerp . Choose Path . Set a clear Lerp Start and Lerp Time. Draw from left toward the middle. Move back to the left. Continue toward the right edge. Example: START ───────→ ←──── ─────────→ END The leftward part reads earlier source-time again. Add A/B movement Vertical position still controls A/B blend. So one Path can shape both dimensions: B /----\ / \__ A ______/ \____ →→→→ ←← →→→→ The IR can move toward B while going forward, return toward earlier source-time, then continue forward with a different A/B balance. Use the waveforms as landmarks A and B are visible behind the Path editor. Use those waveforms like a map. If you can see a strong event, tail or gap, you can deliberately route the Path through it, return to it, or move toward the other source at exactly that point. This makes Path useful for designed time movement , not only abstract drawing. Use N for precise reversals Enable N . Move an internal node left past another x position. The Path keeps its authored order, so that leftward section remains a backward-time route. S keeps the route S smooths the A/B movement without removing the forward/backward time travel. Use it when the vertical blend feels jagged but the timing route is already good. Reset Press R for a straight forward A→B Path. That removes the extra backtracking and returns to normal forward time. Listen for Path can create: repeated internal events reversed fragments inside a forward IR stretched-feeling tails without simple time stretching rhythmic returns to an earlier moment A/B changes that happen differently on repeated source-time Why the IR can become longer Every backward section adds travel. A straight route reads the Lerp window once. A route that goes forward, backward and forward again reads part of that window more than once, so the rendered IR becomes longer. Push it further Bake a Path IR and use it as one side of a new Morph. A Path-generated time structure combined later with Spectral, Stereo Slot Swap or Mid/Side Boundary can create responses whose time and stereo structures were designed in separate generations.

title: Color & Texture
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Color & Texture Color and Texture are where one IR can start turning into something it was not before. Color Color makes a changed copy of the current IR and mixes that copy back in. That gives you three simple questions: Time — how different should the copy's timing be? Leave Time near 1.00 for small differences. Move it further away when you want the copy to become obviously shorter or longer. Very small differences around 1.00 can create phasey, metallic or comb-like tone changes because the original IR and its altered copy interfere with each other. Offset — how much later should the copy begin? Small Offset values can make the interference change dramatically. Larger values can feel more like a separate ghost event, reflection or slap inside the IR. Offset ranges from 0–500 ms. The first few milliseconds are useful for phase/comb color; the wider range can create clearly separated reflections and rhythmic spacing. Amount — how much of the copy do you want? Start lower than you think. The useful point is often where you notice the new character without losing the original IR completely. C1 and C2 A and B each have two Color layers. That means you can create one subtle extra layer with C1 and then use C2 for something different—for example: C1 very close in Time for a phasey tone; C2 further away with Offset for a second reflection or texture. Texture Depth Texture repeats the Color idea in generations. Think: Color makes another version. Texture lets that version make another version. 0 = off 1 = one extra generation 2–4 = deeper and denser Start at 1. More depth is not automatically better. Try this: instant phase color Load any IR into A. Enable C1 . Leave Offset at 0. Move C1 Time only slightly away from 1.00 — for example 0.95 or 1.05. Slowly adjust Amount. Tiny Time differences can completely change the tone. The exact useful value depends on the IR. See more Color phase recipes → Random and reset The small Random button beside Color keeps the current file and tries a new Time/Color/Texture treatment. Double-click Color to reset Color and Texture for that slot without replacing the loaded IR. Technical background A Color layer is a time-resampled, delayed and gain-scaled copy of the slot that is summed back with the original. When two closely related versions are combined, their timing differences create frequency-dependent reinforcement and cancellation—what you hear as phasey or comb-like coloration. Texture recursively feeds each new Color generation into the next.

title: Create a Theme from an Image with AI
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Create a Theme from an Image with AI You can create a complete Impulse Anvil theme without manually choosing every color. Use any image whose mood, contrast and color balance you like as a visual reference, then let an AI translate that look into an Impulse Anvil Theme Schema 2 file. Goal Turn a visual reference into a usable Impulse Anvil theme. Examples: a game screenshot album artwork a photograph a UI you like a color palette your own artwork a screenshot of a room, landscape or object with a strong mood The image does not become part of Impulse Anvil. It is only used as a design reference for the theme colors. What you need Impulse Anvil a saved Theme Schema 2 JSON file one reference image an AI that can read both the JSON and the image Build it 1. Save a Theme Schema 2 file Click the current design name to open the DESIGN workspace. Use SAVE AS to save the current design as a new JSON file somewhere easy to find. This gives the AI the exact structure Impulse Anvil expects without changing the selected packaged design in place. 2. Give the AI the JSON and your reference image Upload both files together. Then use a prompt like: Generate an Impulse Anvil Theme Schema 2 that matches the mood, contrast and color relationships of this image. Keep the JSON structure and all required keys exactly compatible with Impulse Anvil. Return only the finished JSON. 3. Replace the JSON content Open the saved theme file in a text editor. Replace its contents with the JSON generated by the AI and save the file. Then open the DESIGN workspace and click IMPORT , or drag the theme JSON directly onto Impulse Anvil. Your new design is ready to try. Make the result more specific Once the first theme works, you can ask for variations. For example: Make the Morph section more prominent while keeping A and B quieter. Keep the same mood but increase readability. Make the highlights less saturated. Give A and B different accents while keeping the whole theme coherent. Make it darker and more minimal. Keep the palette but increase contrast around active controls. Because Theme Schema 2 supports separate colors for A, B, Morph, EQ, EDIT and OUT, the AI can create more than a single global palette. Generate themes without a reference image You can also upload only the Theme Schema 2 JSON and ask: Generate three high-quality Impulse Anvil themes with clearly different moods. Keep the schema fully compatible. Then try them in Anvil and keep the one that fits your music or workspace best. Design for the mood you want to work in The visual design does not change the audio, but it changes how the workspace feels. A dark, restrained theme can feel very different from a bright high-contrast theme. A cold metallic design can suit a different session than a warm, muted one. Theme design is therefore not only decoration. It is a way to make Impulse Anvil feel like your own instrument and workspace . Use references, not copies The strongest results usually come from asking the AI to translate the mood, palette, contrast and hierarchy of an image rather than reproduce someone else's design literally. Keep a small theme library When a generated theme works well: save the JSON; give it a clear name; keep a few different moods available; switch themes when the project or session changes. Over time you can build your own Impulse Anvil design library without needing to design every theme by hand.

text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Creative Workflows This is the tips, tricks and experiments section. The normal manual explains what every part of Anvil does. Creative Workflows answers a different question: What can I actually make with it? These are recipes, not rules. Start with the values shown, then move them by ear. title: Curves, Draw, Path, Glue & Omni
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Curves, Draw, Path, Glue & Omni Draw Path Glue Path The curve system decides how a Morph relationship develops inside the IR. The authored modes share one visual language, but they do not all use the same time rule. Which authored mode should I use? Mode What it authors Time rule Draw A/B or relationship depth Ordinary output timeline Path Depth plus forward/backward source-time Horizontal-distance clock Glue Path Separate source-time pieces appended in order Glue's horizontal route distance; independent of Lerp timing Omni Path Depth plus source-time plus gesture distance 2-D Euclidean arc-length clock Built-in curves Linear Exp Log S-Curve Use these when you want a predictable transition without drawing it. Draw — paint the relationship Draw uses the normal output timeline. Left to right is time; vertical position is A/B or current relationship depth. F can free the endpoints. N exposes precision nodes so the useful shape can be edited without losing the original idea. Path — move through source-time Path separates playback order from source position: right = read later source-time left = revisit earlier source-time up/down = change A/B or current relationship depth Path uses a horizontal-distance clock. Backtracking adds horizontal travel and can make the constructed IR longer. Vertical movement changes depth, but vertical distance alone is not the Path clock. Glue Path — assemble a new timeline from strokes Glue Path is always free. Each stroke can begin and end at its own source position and depth. Strokes are appended in creation order. Horizontal distance decides how much source-time a stroke contributes. Right reads forward; left reads backward. Mouse-up ends that piece. Glue owns its duration independently of Lerp Start and Lerp Time. Omni Path — make the whole gesture become time Omni Path example: the route shape itself helps define the timing. Omni Path keeps the same two axes, but changes how output time is measured. X remains source-time. Right reads later material; left reads earlier material. Y remains A/B or current Morph relationship depth. Y does not become a second source-position axis. Both X and Y displacement consume output time. A vertical stroke can stay around one source-time position while the response moves through A/B or effect depth. Diagonals, loops and reversals naturally add duration because the ordered 2-D route is longer. The invariant: Omni Path does not make Y become source position. X remains source position and Y remains morph/depth. Instead, both X and Y displacement contribute to the amount of output time generated along the ordered path. Lerp Start and Lerp Time with Omni Omni uses the selected Lerp Start and Lerp Time window as its X domain. Lerp Start offsets which source region the entire painted route reads. Lerp Time scales the width of the source window the route spans. Because the renderer converts route travel across that selected span, a larger Lerp Time can also make the same Omni gesture produce a longer output route. The expanded Omni output does not feed back and redefine that source window. The Omni clock Normal Path measures segment travel from horizontal distance. Omni Path measures the Euclidean length of the 2-D segment: Path: distance = abs(dx) Omni Path: distance = hypot(dx, dy) That gives an intuitive 1:1 normalized metric: a full horizontal move is about one selected source span, a full vertical move is about one span, and a full diagonal is about √2 spans before the normal IR safety ceiling is applied. Authoring tools U — local authored-route undo S — smooth the authored depth movement while preserving route order N — precision nodes F — endpoint freedom where the selected authored mode supports it R — reset Global Undo/Redo also records deliberate authored-route gestures as workstation history steps. Preview and Bake Draw, Path, Glue and Omni feed the prepared construction used for Preview and Bake. Omni is not a lighter preview approximation: the same route semantics are used when the response is committed to WAV. Generated responses remain bounded by Impulse Anvil's existing prepared-IR safety ceiling.

title: Draw Your Own A→B Movement
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Draw Your Own A→B Movement Draw is useful when the built-in curves are close, but the transition needs its own rhythm. Goal Create one IR that moves between A and B in a shape you paint yourself. Build it Load A and B. Click Morph . Enable A→B Lerp . Choose a Morph mode. Set Lerp Start and Lerp Time . Choose Draw . Paint the curve. The bottom of the graph is A. The top is B. The A and B waveforms are visible behind the graph, so you can place the transition around recognizable transients, gaps and tails. Try a return movement Draw something like: B /\ /---- / \ / A ----/ \----/ The IR can move toward B, return toward A, then move back toward B later. Make the endpoints less obvious Enable F . Now the IR can begin or finish on a blend instead of pure A/pure B. For example: begin around 30% B move to almost pure B return toward A finish around 60% B Refine with nodes Enable N . Add a node with a double-click, move it precisely, then use: Shift for fine movement Ctrl for very fine movement Use S when a hand-drawn curve needs a smoother transition. Listen for Listen to when the identity changes : does the attack belong to A while the body becomes B? does the middle briefly return to A? does the tail settle into a blend instead of pure B? Push it further Bake the Draw result, load it back into A, then Morph that new IR with something else. That turns one authored movement into raw material for the next generation.

title: Edit
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Edit Edit Focus turns the prepared response into a large scanning and cutting surface. EDIT is your IR scanner and cutter . It lets you search through a long prepared IR or recording, keep only the interesting part, reverse it if you want, and Bake that fragment as a new IR. Start and End Normal slice When Start is before End , Anvil keeps that region and plays it forward. Reverse slice When Start is after End , Anvil keeps the region between them and plays it backwards. Scan one fixed-size window through a recording The small link control between Start and End locks the current window length. Choose a useful size—perhaps 20 ms, 100 ms or 500 ms. Enable the link. Move Start or End. The other endpoint follows automatically. Listen while the window travels through the recording. Stop when you find a useful spot. Bake it if you want that fragment as its own reusable WAV IR. A single long recording can contain many completely different short convolution fingerprints. Fine millisecond movement Shift + drag = fine movement. Ctrl + drag = very fine movement. Hold the modifier before starting the drag. EDIT Random The small Random button in EDIT tries another edit setup automatically. It can choose short or long regions, move the slice, change fades/predelay and sometimes reverse the region. Fade In / Fade Out Use fades when a cut begins or ends too abruptly. 0 ms means exactly 0 ms. That endpoint stays unshaped. This is especially useful for very short IRs, hard transients and exact cuts. Fade Out + The + option flips the fade-out behavior into a swell/stutter-style ending rather than the normal fade toward silence. Pre Adds time before the edited IR begins. Reset EDIT Double-click the EDIT title to return the editing section to its normal defaults. Technical background Start/End are absolute endpoints on the prepared IR. The selected range is resolved first, fades are applied to that slice, and predelay is inserted afterwards. No hidden authored head/tail micro-fade is added when the user fade value is 0 ms.

title: EQ & Output
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 EQ & Output EQ Focus Out Focus This section has two jobs: finish the IR you are building control how the plugin plays on your track The difference matters when you Bake. These change the IR IR In Changes the level going into the final IR-shaping stage. Use this when the actual response you want to Bake is too quiet or too strong. HP / LP Remove unwanted lows or highs from the IR. Tilt A broad darker/brighter control. Bell 1 / 2 / 3 Use the three bell filters when one frequency area needs a more focused change. Width 0.0 = much narrower / toward mono 1.0 = keep the current width 2.0 = wider Width becomes part of the baked IR. Normalize Brings the final IR up to a consistent peak level. Limiter Adds a safety ceiling to the prepared IR. These only change playback Input Changes the dry/input side of what you hear. Wet Level Changes how loud the convolved result plays. Dry / Wet Changes the balance between the original track and convolution. Out Changes the final plugin output level. None of these four become part of the baked WAV. Baked IR too quiet? Change IR In , IR Gain/Normalize, or the actual IR processing. Do not turn up Out expecting the WAV to change. Random and reset EQ Random changes only the EQ. OUT Random tries a broader finishing variation across EDIT, EQ and Width while protecting the main playback level controls. Double-click EQ to reset EQ. Double-click OUT to reset the OUT/utility section. Technical background EQ, Width, final IR Normalize and limiting are applied to the prepared response before it reaches the convolver/export stage. Input, Wet Level, Dry/Wet and final Out are applied later in the track playback path.

title: FAQ
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 FAQ Can I use ordinary recordings as impulse responses? Yes. Impulse Anvil can load compatible audio material and use it as convolution material. Short intentional fragments are usually easier to control than long unedited recordings. Can I take a tiny part from the tail of an IR and export it? Yes. Use Start and End to isolate the region. Link them when you want to scan a fixed-length window through a longer response, then press Bake . Can I reverse only one selected region? Yes. Move Start later than End . The region between the endpoints becomes a reversed slice. Can I morph two IRs and save the result? Yes. Load A and B, click Morph , choose the relationship you want, then press Bake . Can an IR evolve from A to B inside one file? Yes. Enable A→B Lerp . The selected Morph mode and curve define how the response develops from A toward B over time. Are Lerp Start and Lerp Time percentages? No. They are absolute milliseconds . Lerp Start = when the transition begins Lerp Time = how long it takes Lerp Time can be 0 ms for an instant switch. Can I draw my own Morph/Lerp curve? Yes. Choose Draw in the Curve menu and paint the A/B movement directly. Use U/S/N/F/R for Undo, Smooth, precision Nodes, Free endpoints and Reset. Can Draw start or end on a blend instead of pure A/B? Yes. Enable F in Draw. The first and last points can then sit anywhere between A and B. What does Path do? Path controls both A/B blend and source-time travel . Moving right reads later source-time. Moving left reads earlier source-time again, so a Path can create replayed or reversed sections inside the new IR. Why can Path make the IR longer? A straight Path reads the Lerp time span once. Horizontal backtracking adds extra travel through that span, so the rendered IR becomes longer. Does Path work in Bake? Yes. Path Preview and Bake use the same prepared Path result. What are the waveforms behind the Draw/Path graph? They show the current A and B source shapes behind the curve editor. Use them as visual landmarks when drawing transitions or Path routes—for example, to line up a blend change with a transient, return to an earlier event, or follow a tail by eye. Can I load a baked IR back into Anvil? Yes. A Bake is a standard WAV file, so it can become A or B in another design pass. Is there a separate Bake A→B button? No. The current interface uses one Bake button for every prepared state, including Lerp and authored routes such as Draw, Path, Glue and Omni. Does Out change the exported WAV? No. Out is final playback output only. IR In changes the prepared/baked IR level. Does Dry/Wet change the exported WAV? No. Dry/Wet and Wet Level affect how you hear the plugin on the track, not the IR stored by Bake. Does 0 ms Fade still change the endpoint? No. Fade In = 0 ms or Fade Out = 0 ms leaves that endpoint unshaped. How far can Color Offset go? Color Offset runs from 0–500 ms . Tiny offsets are useful for phase/comb tone. Larger values can create clearly separated secondary events. Does Anvil remember where I browse for IRs? Yes. A successful manual load remembers that folder and uses it as the first choice next time. Can I customize A, B and the other panels separately? Yes. Click the current design name to open the DESIGN workspace, choose EDIT COLORS , then enable panel-specific colors for A, B, Morph, EQ, EDIT or OUT. Can I export a theme? Yes. Open the DESIGN workspace and use SAVE AS to write the current design to a new JSON file. That JSON can be edited, shared and imported again. How do I switch between hearing A, B and Morph? Click the A , B or Morph panel. Can I make tiny millisecond adjustments more easily? Yes. Hold Shift before dragging for fine movement or Ctrl before dragging for very fine movement. What can Align remove? Align can shift a source so its important peak begins earlier. If useful material existed before that peak, that pre-peak material can be lost. Compare Align on and off when the lead-in matters. How do I reset only one part of Anvil? Double-click Color , EQ , EDIT or OUT to reset that section. To reset the whole control state while keeping A/B files loaded, use Options → Init / Reset Controls (keep IRs) .

A fast double-click can therefore select the panel on the first click before Focus opens; that is intentional in the current interaction model. Exit Focus Use the Focus control again. Press Esc. Click the exposed outer plugin background. Double-click empty Focus background. What changes? Only the presentation. The active parameters, IRs, Morph mode, Draw/Path/Glue/Omni state, preview and project state remain the same. Morph Focus Morph gets a larger authoring canvas. With A→B Lerp enabled, the left side can show the prepared FINAL IR waveform while the curve remains available on the right. Why use it? Stay in Overview while making broad decisions. Enter Focus when one curve, waveform, EQ move or source treatment deserves precision, then return without losing the signal-path context.

title: Found Sounds as IR Material
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Found Sounds as IR Material A recording does not need to be a measured room response to become useful convolution material. The easiest way to understand this is simply to try it. Good first recordings Record something with a clear character: metal, glass or ceramic hits; cloth, paper or leaves; doors, tools and mechanical objects; water, gravel or footsteps; a clap or snap in an unusual room; a breath or short vocal sound; a short noise or texture. Build it Load the recording into A . Click A so you are hearing it. Use Start/End to isolate one interesting region. Link Start and End if you want to scan a fixed-size window through the recording. Fade the edges if the cut feels too abrupt. Try Color or Texture. Use EQ only if the material needs cleanup. Bake several promising versions. Listen for the small moments A long recording may sound obviously like "a recording." A tiny part of the same file can behave like something completely different: a resonant filter; a strange cabinet; a sharp transient space; a metallic tonal fingerprint; a tiny impossible room. That is why EDIT is so useful with found sounds. Scan instead of guessing Create a short Start/End window and link it. Then move the window through the recording while audio plays. Shift + drag = fine Ctrl + drag = very fine When a position suddenly does something interesting to the track, stop and Bake it. Push it further Take one good fragment and: phase-color it with Color ; Morph it with a normal room IR; Bake it and use it again; create several different fragments from the same recording and Morph those together. Capturing a resonant object? For guitars, violins, cabinets and other resonant bodies, continue with Acoustic Bodies & Comparison . It explains what a body IR can transfer, how to compare two matched captures and why one IR should not be treated as a complete physical clone of the instrument.

title: Impulse Anvil
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Impulse Anvil THE IR IS THE THING YOU ARE MAKING Impulse Anvil is an impulse-response design workstation . Load IRs, recordings or found sounds as material, decide how A and B should relate, then Bake the response you make into a reusable WAV. 1. Your sound goes in. A vocal, drum, synth, guitar, field recording or anything else on the track. 2. An IR changes it. The response can add filtering, resonance, space, reflections or stranger transformations. 3. Anvil changes the IR. A and B are material. Morph defines their relationship. Draw, Path, Glue and Omni can author how that relationship develops. 4. Bake keeps the result. Your experiment becomes a reusable WAV impulse response. The useful mental shortcut: when you reshape the IR, you reshape the transformation that will be applied to your sound. Material → Relationship → Movement → Sculpt → Bake A and B provide material, Morph defines their relationship, the authoring tools control movement, Edit/EQ/Output refine the result, and Bake keeps it. Where do you want to start? Make something in 5 minutes Get from an empty plugin to your first useful Bake without learning the whole manual. Learn Anvil by doing Enter the focused Basics Course and learn Anvil one hands-on task at a time. Your progress stays on this device. Choose the A/B relationship Start with the human idea behind each Morph mode, then open Technical details only when you want them. Try creative recipes Use focused examples when you want a destination instead of another control description. How these docs teach The learning pages use one information order: Why → Do → Notice → Understand → Technical details You should be allowed to understand the idea before you are expected to know the specialist vocabulary. Reference pages stay compact for returning users. Technical words with a dotted underline can be hovered, focused with the keyboard or clicked to reveal a short explanation. These definitions are optional; they are not prerequisites for continuing.

title: IR A / IR B
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 IR A / IR B A Focus gives one source room for Time, Gain, Color, Texture and source navigation. A and B are two independent source lanes. They can hold measured IRs, designed IRs or compatible recordings. Choose what you are listening to The current interface uses the panels themselves as navigation: click A to hear A; click B to hear B; click Morph to hear A and B through the current Morph setup. There is no separate user-facing "A Only" / "B Only" workflow to learn. Load a source Use Load or drag a WAV/AIFF/FLAC file directly onto the A or B panel. The whole card accepts drops. Use the previous/next arrows to step through discovered IR files. Time A / Time B Changes the duration of that source before Color, Texture and Morph. Below 1.0 = shorter/faster. 1.0 = original duration. Above 1.0 = longer/slower. Normalize A / Normalize B A and B have independent Normalize switches . Turn Normalize on when one source is much quieter or louder than the other and you want a more even starting point before Morph. Gain Gain still works even with Normalize enabled . Normalize creates the reference level first; Gain lets you intentionally make A or B more dominant afterwards. Random discovery Random beside Load Chooses another available IR and randomizes the slot's Time, Color and Texture . It does not randomly boost Gain: Gain returns to 0 dB . Your Normalize switch stays as you set it. Random beside Color Keeps the current file but randomizes its Time, Color and Texture settings. Use it when you like the source itself but want a new treatment. Reset the slot's creative layer Double-click the Color header in A or B to reset that slot's Color and Texture controls without replacing the loaded source. Technical background The slot processing order is Time → Color/Texture → per-slot Normalize → Gain. During two-slot processing, sample-rate differences are resolved as required before A/B construction.

title: Learn Impulse Anvil by Doing
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Hands-on learning Learn Impulse Anvil by Doing You don't have to study the plugin before you use it. The Basics Course teaches it one small action at a time while you have Impulse Anvil open. START WITH A SOUND You don't need to know what an IR is But I want to know In Impulse Anvil, any WAV can become an IR. Kick, hi-hat, shaker, clap, noise, a bad recording artifact — whatever. You can also use AIF, AIFF and FLAC. If your DAW has a file browser, you can drag a sound straight onto A or B. You can also record your own sounds: scratch a surface, record water, room noise, a strange object, or anything else that gives you an interesting shape. For the first few lessons, try a sound or IR around one second long . Longer or shorter works too — this just makes the changes easy to hear. IMPULSE ANVIL BASICS COURSE START COURSE 34 hands-on lessons · progress stays on this device A → Shape → B → Morph → A→B Lerp → Bake again. Full-workstation course: later lessons use Texture Depth, Color 2, Bake, the full Morph collection and A→B Lerp. Using the free demo? Start with the 5-Minute Quickstart . What happens inside the course? Only the current lesson stays on screen. Finish it, mark it Done, and the next one unlocks. You can always go back or open the course overview, but future lessons stay locked until you reach them. When you finish all 34 lessons, Course Mode gives you a small local completion certificate with the date, time and your active course duration. You can save it as a PNG if you want.

title: Morph & A→B Lerp
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Morph & A→B Lerp The Morph browser groups the relationship library and lets you inspect the selected mode. A Morph mode answers one question: what relationship should Anvil create between A and B? The Morph amount controls how far you move into that relationship. Draw, Path, Glue and Omni can then make the relationship change through the response instead of staying at one fixed amount. If you are new: start with Time Morph . It is the baseline. Every other mode is easier to understand once you have heard the straightforward version first. Demo / full-license note: the free demo includes Time Morph . The full license unlocks the rest of the Morph relationship library, A→B Lerp/Draw/Path/Glue/Omni and WAV baking. The cards below document the complete workstation so demo users can still see what each full relationship is for. Choose by intention I just want A to become B. Start with Time Morph. I want their tonal character to combine differently. Try Spectral, BandSwap or ZigZag. I want to hear what they share. Try Common. I want to hear what separates them. Try Aligned Difference, Matched Residual or Difference Focus. I want something deliberately unnatural. Try Ghost, Eclipse, Nest or Spectral Time Shear. I want the relationship to move inside the IR. Choose a mode first, then use Lerp, Draw, Path, Glue or Omni. Core Morph — move or redistribute A and B Time Morph Move directly between A and B. Listen for: the clearest, most literal A-to-B transition. It is the easiest reference point for every other mode. Try it when: you want to understand two new source responses before getting experimental. Technical details Direct sample-by-sample movement between the prepared A and B responses. Spectral Move more of the frequency character of A toward B. Listen for: a tonal change that can feel different from a direct waveform blend. Try it when: A and B have obviously different dark, bright, resonant or filtered characters. Technical details Moves the frequency-magnitude structure of A toward B while maintaining a stable phase relationship. Spectral BandSwap Let A control some broad frequency areas and B control others. Listen for: hybrids where lows, mids and highs can feel as if they come from different sources. Try it when: you want a more obviously constructed hybrid instead of a smooth blend. Technical details Alternates broad spectral bands between A and B and swaps their ownership through Morph. Spectral ZigZag Interleave A and B more tightly across frequency. Listen for: sharper, fractured and more synthetic hybrids. Try it when: BandSwap is interesting but still feels too broad or orderly. Technical details Uses denser alternating spectral stripes for a more finely interleaved frequency relationship. Stereo Slot Swap Make the left and right sides travel through A and B in opposite directions. Listen for: asymmetrical width and stereo movement. Try it when: the two responses have interesting stereo differences. Technical details Sends the A/B relationship in opposite directions across left and right channels. Mid/Side Boundary Keep more of A in the center while B increasingly defines the sides. Listen for: a stable middle with a different texture or space around it. Try it when: you want width without making the center disappear. Technical details Uses Mid/Side structure so A remains more of the center/mid anchor while B increasingly defines the outside/side field. Residual / Decompose — ask what they share and what separates them A residual is simply what remains after some estimated part has been removed. These modes are most useful when you stop thinking “blend A and B” and start thinking “what is actually different here?” Raw Difference Subtract one response from the other exactly as they are. Listen for: remaining differences, plus potentially strong combing or ringing when timing/level do not match. Try it when: you want the most literal and potentially unruly version of “what is different?” Technical details Literal directional subtraction. Timing and level mismatches remain part of the result. Aligned Difference Line up the main events first, then subtract. Listen for: less of the difference caused only by arrival timing and more of what remains afterward. Try it when: A and B are related captures whose important hit/event does not start at exactly the same point. Technical details Aligns the dominant events of A and B before directional subtraction. Matched Residual Line them up, bring their overall levels closer, then hear what remains. Listen for: differences that are less dominated by simple timing and broadband loudness mismatch. Try it when: you are comparing related responses recorded at slightly different levels. Technical details Aligns and broadband level-matches the responses before subtraction. Spectral Carve Carve the reference away by different amounts at different frequencies. Listen for: differences that appear in specific low, mid or high regions instead of one uniform subtraction. Try it when: two responses feel similar overall but clearly differ in particular frequency areas. Technical details Uses bounded frequency-dependent subtraction instead of removing the same amount everywhere. Similarity Residual Remove more where A and B already appear similar. Listen for: contrasting material becoming more exposed as shared-looking regions are reduced. Try it when: the sources are related enough that a plain subtraction feels too crude. Technical details Removes the reference more strongly where A and B appear genuinely similar. Common Keep more of what A and B appear to share. Listen for: a response that can feel like a shared core with some unique material reduced. Try it when: A and B are related rooms, resonances, captures or variations of similar material. Technical details Estimates the response component shared by A and B. Unique A Keep more of what makes A different from B. Listen for: A's contrasting material after estimated shared content is reduced. Try it when: A and B are similar and you want to explore what separates A from B. Technical details Keeps what remains characteristic of A after estimated shared material is removed. Unique B Keep more of what makes B different from A. Listen for: B's contrasting material after estimated shared content is reduced. Try it when: B contains a resonance, space or texture you want to examine without simply crossfading all of B over A. Technical details Keeps what remains characteristic of B after estimated shared material is removed. Difference Focus Turn the disagreement up and the agreement down. Listen for: the regions where A and B contrast most strongly becoming more obvious. Try it when: you want a more exaggerated difference rather than a literal residual. Technical details Emphasizes regions where the two responses disagree most strongly. Spectro-Temporal Residual Find differences that change across both time and frequency. Listen for: local fragments and textures that can appear only at particular moments or frequency regions. Try it when: the interesting difference is not constant through the whole response. Technical details Varies similarity and subtraction locally across both time and frequency. Acoustic Interaction — make the responses operate on each other Nest Pass one acoustic response through the other. Listen for: a combined response that behaves more like stacked acoustic systems than a crossfade. Try it when: the idea of “cabinet through room” or “resonant object through space” is more interesting than blending. Technical details Cascades A and B as acoustic transfer functions, effectively placing one response through the other. Transfer Estimate the filter-like transformation that moves one response toward the other. Listen for: the relationship between the sources becoming the material, rather than either source by itself. Try it when: A and B are related enough that “what changes A into B?” is an interesting question. Technical details Builds a stabilized A→B or B→A transfer operator. This is an estimated DSP relationship, not semantic recognition of the physical source. Ghost Use the tonal shape of one response with the phase structure of the other. Listen for: a familiar frequency body behaving with a different internal timing/phase character. Try it when: A and B have very different tonal and temporal personalities. Technical details Combines the magnitude structure of one response with the phase structure of the other. Eclipse Push A and B toward deep cancellation, then keep what survives. Listen for: hollow, carved, sparse or unstable responses. Try it when: A and B are related and you want something more extreme than an ordinary difference mode. Technical details Searches for a stable deep-cancellation relationship and keeps the surviving residual. Spectral Time Shear Let lows, mids and highs follow different A/B journeys through time. Listen for: a response whose frequency regions seem to evolve on different timelines. Try it when: you want motion that is more complex than the whole spectrum moving together. Technical details Creates a time-frequency hybrid where low, mid and high regions follow different A/B trajectories. Direction matters in some modes Some Residual and Acoustic Interaction modes expose a small direction control because “A relative to B” is not the same question as “B relative to A.” Unique A and Unique B already state their direction in the name. Choose the relationship, then author its behavior A fixed Morph amount chooses one position in the selected relationship. Built-in curves, Draw, Path, Glue and Omni can turn that amount into movement through the response. Draw: paint how relationship depth changes. Path: also route which point in source-time is read, including backward travel. Glue Path: assemble separate painted pieces into a new sequence; Glue owns its constructed duration independently of Lerp Start/Time. Omni Path: keep X as source-time and Y as relationship depth while both horizontal and vertical route travel create output time inside the selected Lerp source window. Learn Draw, Path, Glue and Omni → A→B Lerp A→B Lerp builds one static IR whose internal relationship changes over time. It is not a DAW automation recording. The selected Morph mode and authored curve/path become part of the prepared response, and Bake can commit that construction to WAV. Technical background The longer prepared A/B endpoint defines the main Lerp source domain. Absolute Lerp Start and Time are clamped to the available endpoint duration. Time Morph can run as a continuous time-varying blend; spectral/spatial relationships use mode-aware rendering so Preview and Bake share the same prepared result. Try it instead of memorizing it You do not need to learn 21 definitions before using Morph. Load two contrasting responses, start with Time Morph, switch one mode at a time and listen to what question each mode asks differently. Open the Guided Learning quests →

title: Multi-Morph Stereo Worlds
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Multi-Morph Stereo Worlds One Morph does not have to be the end of the design. Because Anvil can Bake the result, you can create one stereo relationship, freeze it into a new IR, then combine that new IR with another differently built response. This is multi-morphing . Basic multi-morph Goal Build a response whose stereo and tonal behavior comes from more than one Morph generation. Build it Load A and B. Choose Stereo Slot Swap . Move Morph toward a useful A-left / B-right relationship rather than automatically centering it. Bake that result as IR 1 . Create another result from two sources—new ones or the same ones. Use a different Morph mode. Bake it as IR 2 . Load IR 1 into A and IR 2 into B. Morph those two Bakes again—for example with Spectral . Bake the new generation. What happened? The last Morph is no longer working with two simple source IRs. It is working with two already-designed soundfields . That is why the result can become much more complex than one Morph pass. Advanced recipe — Stereo Slot Swap + Mid/Side Boundary + Spectral This is a strong starting recipe for very large or unusual stereo responses. Stage 1 — build a left/right relationship Load two interesting IRs. Choose Stereo Slot Swap . Find a position where the A/B relationship gives you useful left/right contrast. Bake it as StereoSwap.wav . Stereo Slot Swap lets the left side travel A→B while the right side travels B→A, so the two sides can carry different source relationships. Stage 2 — build a center/side relationship Load two other sources—or reuse the same ones with different settings. Choose Mid/Side Boundary . Find a position where A gives you a strong center and B gives you an interesting outside field. Bake it as MidSide.wav . Stage 3 — morph the two finished soundfields Load StereoSwap.wav into A. Load MidSide.wav into B. Start with Time Morph just to hear the two complete structures together. Then try Spectral . Move Morph slowly. Bake anything that creates a stereo world you could not get from either generation alone. Why this can become huge You are combining: a response where left and right already carry different A/B relationships; a response with a deliberate center/side structure; then a third Morph operation that combines those finished responses again. The result can contain a dense center, different side information, and spectral changes across a stereo field that was already complex before the final Morph began. Do not chase maximum width Huge does not always mean useful. Check the result in context with your track and pull Width back if the center starts feeling weak or disconnected. Push it further After the final Bake: put the result back into A and add a room IR in B; use Color with tiny Time differences on only one generation; use EDIT to keep only the best section of the final stereo response; reverse a fragment; create two branches and Morph those branches again. That is the point where an IR can become a designed sound world rather than a recognizable mixture of its original sources. Technical background Stereo Slot Swap processes the left field from A toward B while the right field travels from B toward A. Mid/Side Boundary keeps A as the center foundation while B contributes the side field. Baking each stage collapses that processing into new stereo IR data, so a later Morph treats the already-complex outputs as new source material.

title: Phase & Comb Textures with Color
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Phase & Comb Textures with Color Color can do much more than create obvious echoes or extra layers. When the Color copy is almost the same length and timing as the original IR , the two versions interfere with each other. Tiny movements can create large tonal changes. This works with almost any IR. Recipe 1 — Time-only phase color Goal Create a phasey, metallic or comb-like version of an IR without using Offset. Build it Load an IR into A . Click A so you are hearing that slot. Enable C1 . Keep Offset at 0 ms . Move C1 Time slightly away from 1.00 . Try small differences first: around 0.99 / 1.01 , then 0.95 / 1.05 , then further if useful. Adjust Amount by ear. Listen for Do not listen for "more reverb." Listen for the tone itself bending : hollowness, metallic peaks, notches, nasal colors, widening/narrowing impressions, or a completely different cabinet-like character. Tip The important thing is the difference from 1.00 , not one magic value. A tiny change can be dramatic on one IR and subtle on another. Recipe 2 — Offset-only comb color Goal Keep the Color copy at the same length but move it slightly later. Build it Enable C1. Keep Time at 1.00 . Move Offset slowly from about 1–20 ms . Adjust Amount. Listen for Very small offsets can sound like tonal filtering rather than a separate echo. As Offset gets larger, the extra copy starts to feel more like a distinct reflection. Recipe 3 — Mixed Time + Offset phasing Goal Create a less predictable interference pattern by changing both the length and position of the Color copy. Build it Start with C1 Time only slightly different from 1.00 — for example 0.95 or 1.05 . Add a tiny Offset, roughly 1–20 ms . Move Time by very small amounts. Move Offset again. Keep alternating between the two until you hit a useful pocket. Listen for This is where the tone can become very complex because the copy is both drifting in time and starting from a different position . Small movements matter more than large ones. Add C2 Once C1 gives you a useful color: enable C2; keep one Color layer subtle; let the other one use a different Time or Offset relationship. You can create two different interference patterns inside the same IR before Texture or Morph even begins. Add Texture carefully Texture repeats the Color transformation in generations. With a phasey Color setup, even Depth 1 or 2 can become very dense. Do not assume higher Depth is better. Stop when the character becomes useful. Bake the sweet spot If one tiny combination sounds special, Bake it. You can then use that phase-colored IR as new source material instead of trying to remember the exact settings. Technical background Color mixes a time-resampled and optionally delayed copy of the IR back with the original. When two related signals differ by small amounts in time, some frequencies reinforce while others cancel. The result is frequency-dependent comb filtering. Changing Color Time makes that relationship evolve across the IR instead of behaving like a single fixed delay.

title: Recursive Baking
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Recursive Baking A Bake does not have to be the final result. It can become the next ingredient . The basic idea Make something: A + B → Bake C Then load C back into Anvil: C + D → Bake E Then do it again: E + recording F → Bake G By G, the original ingredients may no longer be obvious at all. Build it Create a useful A/B result. Bake it. Load that Bake back into A. Put a different source in B. Change the Morph mode, Color, EDIT region or stereo treatment. Bake again. Do not make only one lineage Instead of: A+B → C → D → E → F try branches: A+B → C1 A+B → C2 C1 + metal → D1 C2 + room → D2 D1 + D2 → E Branches give you more different material to recombine later. Keep generations under control Recursive design can quickly become dense. When that happens: use EDIT to keep only the useful section; Normalize deliberately; use HP/LP to remove useless buildup; compare against an earlier generation; stop adding layers when the new Bake is only "more" rather than better. Strong combination Recursive Baking becomes especially powerful with Multi-Morph Stereo Worlds , because each generation can preserve a different spatial relationship before the next Morph begins.

title: Technical Background
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Technical Background This section collects implementation details that are useful for deeper reference. The normal feature pages remain producer-facing. Slot preparation order time stretch Color / Texture construction optional per-slot Normalize slot Gain Gain therefore remains meaningful while a slot's Normalize switch is enabled. Color Color resamples the source to create a time-scaled copy, applies a sample offset and gain, then sums that copy back with the source. Color Offset now has a 0–500 ms user range. Texture Texture is recursive Color. Each generated layer becomes input to the next generation. Depth is 0–4. Time Morph and Align Time Morph interpolates sample values between A and B. Align can left-shift participating time-domain material toward sample zero. Material that originally occurred before the moved peak can therefore be lost. Spectral Morph Spectral modes transform the sources into frequency-domain representations, combine spectral information, and reconstruct a causal response. Absolute Lerp timing Impulse Anvil uses Lerp Start and Lerp Time in milliseconds. The visible UI domain follows the current prepared A/B endpoint duration, including Time and Color/Texture length growth. Start reduces the remaining available Time range. Draw Draw stores a normalized A/B curve. With Free off, the first point is A=0 and the last point is B=1. With Free on, the first/last y values may sit anywhere from 0–1. Outside the active Lerp timing window, the authored free endpoint value is held. Path Path stores an ordered list of normalized (x, y) points: x = source-time position inside the Lerp window y = A/B blend point order = output traversal order The renderer accumulates absolute horizontal travel. Leftward x movement is preserved, so earlier source-time is read again rather than being sorted away. A straight 0→1 path uses the normal span. Backtracking adds output frames. Exact endpoints Hidden authored head/tail micro-fades were removed from the Color/preview/prepared paths. A user Fade value of 0 ms leaves that endpoint unshaped. Runtime convolver switching remains click-protected separately. Post/Sculpt order slice/reverse → fades → predelay → IR In → HP/LP/Bells/Tilt → Width → Normalize → IR-side limiter Final Dry/Wet mixing, Wet Level and final Out happen later and are not part of Bake. Theme Schema 2 Global colors remain the base theme. A, B, Morph, EQ, EDIT and OUT may each optionally override panel, panelStroke, accent, highlight, knob and text colors. Disabled panel overrides inherit Global values.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 Troubleshooting Bake says “Nothing to export” A prepared IR is not ready yet. Load A, or load A+B and enable Morph/A→B Lerp. If you just made a heavy change, let the preview finish rebuilding and press Bake again. A change takes longer on a long IR Controls that rebuild the impulse response may need to process many samples, spectral transforms and recursive Color/Texture layers. Trim the useful region earlier when possible. My Bake level does not follow Out That is expected. Out is playback-only . Use IR In , slot gains or IR Normalize when you want to change the exported response level. Texture does nothing Texture needs an enabled Color transformation. Set Texture Depth above 0 and enable C1 or C2 in that same slot. A→B Lerp disabled the Morph knob That is intentional. Lerp is not a single global A/B position; it changes state across the IR's own time axis. Curve, K and Lerp Time define that progression. My external source does not restore in an old project Impulse Anvil stores file paths for externally loaded IRs. Keep the files available at the same location or reload them manually.

title: Turn a 2-D Gesture into Time with Omni Path
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Workflow Turn a 2-D Gesture into Time with Omni Path Omni Path example in the Morph panel. Omni Path makes the gesture itself part of the clock. Move sideways and you travel through source-time. Move vertically and time still passes. That means you can hold around one moment of the source while the A/B or Morph relationship changes. Goal Create an IR whose internal duration follows the distance of a two-dimensional route rather than only its left/right travel. Know what the axes mean X = source-time. Right reads later material; left reads earlier material. Y = A/B or current Morph relationship depth. Output time = distance travelled through the 2-D route. Omni does not turn Y into source-time. X and Y keep their normal jobs. The new part is that movement on both axes consumes output time. Lerp Start and Lerp Time Lerp Start offsets the source region the entire painted route reads. Lerp Time scales the width of the source-time window the route spans. Because output route frames are derived from travelled distance across that span, a larger Lerp Time can also make the same gesture yield a longer output route. Glue Path does not use this window. Omni Path does. Build it Load different material into A and B. Activate Morph and enable A→B Lerp . Choose the Morph relationship you want to explore. Set a clear Lerp Start and Lerp Time . Choose Omni Path . Draw a simple route first, then Preview it. Try four gestures 1. Horizontal Draw mostly left-to-right at a steady Y position. This behaves closest to ordinary source traversal because almost all route distance comes from X. 2. Vertical hold At roughly the middle of the graph, draw almost straight upward or downward. Source-time stays around that X position while A/B or relationship depth changes. Unlike normal Path or Glue's vertical-only behavior, this vertical distance creates real output duration. 3. Diagonal Move through source-time and depth together. Because both axes contribute to distance, a large diagonal takes longer than a purely horizontal move of the same width. 4. Loop or reverse Move right, rise, go left, then continue. Reversals revisit earlier source material; vertical and diagonal parts add their own travel. Path vs Omni Path Path = horizontal-distance clock Omni Path = 2-D arc-length clock Both can move backward through source-time. The difference is that ordinary Path only derives elapsed route time from horizontal travel, while Omni also counts vertical movement. Glue Path vs Omni Path Glue Path assembles independent strokes as separate pieces and owns its duration independently of Lerp Start/Time. Omni Path uses free multi-stroke authoring inside the selected Lerp source window, but its clock follows the complete 2-D route. Technical background For each route segment, normal Path uses horizontal travel: distance = abs(dx) Omni Path uses normalized Euclidean 2-D travel: distance = hypot(dx, dy) The renderer walks that cumulative arc length uniformly. At each output point, X chooses the source index and Y chooses the blend/effect depth. Persisted route geometry, not mouse drawing speed, determines the result. Preview and Bake Preview and Bake use the same Omni route semantics. When a gesture produces something useful, Bake commits the prepared construction as a reusable WAV IR.

title: What Gets Baked?
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 What Gets Baked? There is one rule worth learning: Some controls change the IR you are making. Other controls only change how you hear the plugin. These become part of the IR A/B → Time → Color / Texture → Slot Normalize → Slot Gain → Morph / Lerp → EDIT → IR In → EQ → Width → Normalize → Limiter → Bake If you change something in that chain, you are changing the response that can be saved. These are only for playback The following controls do not become part of the baked WAV: Input Wet Level Dry / Wet Out They only change how Anvil sounds on the track while you are working. Simple example If the WAV you Bake is too quiet, change IR In or the IR's Normalize/Gain path. Turning up Out only makes the plugin louder while you listen; it does not make the exported IR louder. Technical background Anvil prepares and caches the processed impulse response before final track playback. Dry/wet mixing and final output gain happen afterwards, so they cannot change the exported IR data.

title: What Impulse Anvil Does
text: Impulse Anvil 1.0.122 Windows VST3 What Impulse Anvil Does Impulse Anvil is for making impulse responses , not only loading them. A normal convolution workflow is often: pick an IR → put sound through it Anvil adds the creative part before that: load IRs or recordings → change them → combine them → listen → Bake a new IR You can start with almost anything useful Try: a room or cabinet IR; another IR you already designed; a metal hit; a voice or breath; a scrape; a field recording; a short noise or texture; a tiny section taken from a much longer recording. The source does not need to sound like a reverb before you load it. What Anvil lets you do A and B hold two independent starting materials. Time makes them shorter or longer. Color adds changed copies back into the IR. Texture repeats that Color idea in deeper layers. Morph decides how A and B become one new response. A→B Lerp lets the IR itself move from A toward B over time. EDIT searches, cuts, reverses and fades the part you actually want. EQ and Width shape the final IR. Bake saves what you made as a reusable WAV. Why Bake matters Bake turns an experiment into new raw material. You can make: A + B → C then load C back in: C + D → E and continue. That is why Impulse Anvil can create results that no single original IR contained. Technical background Convolution can use any compatible audio waveform as its impulse-response data. Short material often behaves more like a complex tonal/filter fingerprint; longer material can add stronger time, resonance and decay behavior. Anvil uses that freedom deliberately for sound design instead of limiting the source material to measured acoustic spaces.
